title: Saraswati: The Flowing Word
summary: A devotional month with Saraswati, river of the Rig Veda and goddess of knowledge, speech and music. Learn her names and image, her hymns and history, how Vasant Panchami and the Saraswati Puja of Navaratri are kept, and how to offer white flowers, a lamp and your own study at a simple home puja, then decide whether to make a personal vow of devotion.
welcome:
This journey spends about a lunar month learning about Saraswati and offering her simple devotion (bhakti) at home. She is honoured by Hindus everywhere, and by Jains and Buddhists too: by children writing their first letters, by students before an exam, by musicians before they play, and by whole schools and colleges on her festival day.

You will learn her names and image, her life as a river and a goddess of speech in the Vedas, how she has been worshipped in India and beyond, how her festivals are kept, and how to make a small home puja with white flowers, a lamp, and your books, pens or instrument. For seven days you will make your study and practice an offering to her, ending as many families do, by beginning again with a first letter. At the end you may make a personal vow of devotion, or not.

Please read this plainly. This is not an initiation. Formal initiation (dīkṣā) and mantras traditionally given by a guru are not offered here and cannot be given by an app. Nothing here is "magic", an exam charm or a spell; it is devotion. The best thing this journey can do is send you to a temple, a Saraswati Puja or a Hindu friend's home, and above all to a good teacher, to learn from the people whose religion this is.
about: Saraswati (Sarasvatī, "she who has flowing waters" or "she of the pools") is the Hindu goddess of knowledge, learning, speech, music and the arts. In the Rig Veda she is first a great river, praised as the best of mothers, rivers and goddesses; in later Vedic texts she is identified with Vac, sacred speech, and so becomes the goddess of the word and of all learning. In the Puranas she is the consort of Brahma, the creator; in Bengal she is one of Durga's daughters who come home at Durga Puja. She is pictured dressed in white, seated on a white lotus, playing the veena (a stringed instrument) and holding a book and a rosary, with a swan (hamsa) and sometimes a peacock beside her. Her great festival is Vasant Panchami in late winter; in the south she is worshipped in the last days of Navaratri, when books and instruments are laid before her and children begin their letters on Vijayadashami. She is also honoured by Jains as the goddess of scripture, and in Buddhist Asia, where in Japan she became Benzaiten.
notes: Hinduism is a living religion. Saraswati belongs first to the Hindu families, temples and teachers who worship her. This journey is a respectful introduction and an invitation to learn from them, not a replacement.

Dīkṣā (formal initiation) and mantras traditionally given by a guru are not offered here. Where Hindu prayers are mentioned, the app gives its own English words. Learn Sanskrit prayers, and their pronunciation and proper use, from a priest, teacher or family.

This is devotion, not magic. Saraswati is not an exam charm or a study hack. Please do not use her, her image or her names in spells or as décor. Her devotees honour her above all by real effort: study, practice and respect for teachers.

In Hindu custom books, paper, pens and instruments are treated with respect as belonging to her: they are not stepped on or touched with the feet, and if one is, it is touched to the forehead in apology. This journey asks you to keep that custom.
Offerings are vegetarian: no meat, fish, eggs or alcohol. White and yellow flowers, milk sweets and fruit are hers.
Treat her image with care: keep it raised, clean and out of bathrooms; do not put it on shoes, floor mats or anything you sit on.

The app can show the Hindu lunar calendar (panchang): tick it under "Also show" in "Calendar & holidays". It marks Sharad Navaratri, whose last days include Saraswati Puja, and Purnima. Vasant Panchami you will find in a printed panchang. Panchangs, regions and countries can differ by a day; confirm with your local temple.
Safety: keep lamps and incense well away from books, paper and cloth. Some kumkum powders have been found to contain lead; buy lead-free and keep them from children.

stages.title: A Clean Page
stages.intro: Begin by learning who Saraswati is, set up a small clean shrine beside the place where you study or practise, and offer a first simple puja: a lamp, a white flower, and a book or pen laid before her.

lessons.title: The Goddess in White
lessons.summary: Her names, her image and what it shows, and what Hindus mean by the knowledge she gives.

sections.heading: Her names
sections.body:
Saraswati (Sarasvatī) is usually explained as "she who has pools" or "she who flows", from saras, a lake or flowing water. She was first a river, and the sense of flowing never left her: speech flows, music flows, and so does understanding when it comes.

She has many other names. Vani and Vagdevi mean "speech" and "goddess of speech"; Sharada, "the autumnal one", is her name at the great temple of Sringeri and in Kashmir; Bharati is "the eloquent"; Vidyadayini, "giver of knowledge"; Veenapani, "she who holds the veena"; Hamsavahini, "she who rides the swan". Lists of her 108 names are recited by devotees.

sections.heading: Reading her image
sections.body:
Saraswati is almost always dressed in white, the colour of purity and clarity, and seated on a white lotus or a rock by water. She usually has four arms. Two hands play the veena, a long-necked stringed instrument. One holds a book, the Vedas or all learning; one holds a rosary (mala), for prayer and concentration; sometimes she holds a small pot of water. Beside her is a swan (hamsa), and often a peacock.

Devotees and teachers read these details with love. The swan is said to be able to separate milk from water, and so stands for discernment, telling the true from the false. The book is knowledge, the veena the arts, the rosary inner discipline. Some of these readings are old and some modern; all are taught to children in Hindu homes.

sections.heading: Knowledge as something holy
sections.body:
Hindu tradition distinguishes two kinds of knowledge: the knowledge of this world, of arts, crafts, sciences and languages, and the knowledge that frees, of the self and of God. Saraswati is honoured as the giver of both. That is why a schoolchild, a music student and a philosopher all bow to her.

It also explains a custom you will see everywhere. Books, paper and pens are treated as hers. A child who drops a book picks it up and touches it to the forehead. Musicians touch their instrument and bow before they play. Learning is not only useful; it is a gift, and something to be received with humility.

sections.heading: Starting in the right place
sections.body:
It is easy to treat Saraswati as a mascot for study, a pretty image on a desk. For Hindus she is the Mother, the goddess who gives speech and understanding, worshipped with love every day. That should shape how you come to her: learn first, ask before you join in, and treat her image, and your own books and instruments, as you would treat something holy of your own.

Her festival is one of the most welcoming in the Hindu year. Schools, colleges and neighbourhoods hold Saraswati Puja, and students are glad to show visitors what they do. If you can, go and see one.

knowAndDont.known: Her names, her white-clad image with veena, book, rosary and swan, her identification with speech (Vac), and the customs of respect toward books and instruments are universal in living practice and attested in Vedic and Puranic texts.
knowAndDont.unknown: The derivation of her name is explained in several ways. Popular readings of each detail of her image, such as the swan separating milk from water, are traditional teaching whose age is hard to fix; the milk-and-water story itself is old in Indian literature, but its link to her image may be later.

lessons.inPractice: Find an image of Saraswati you can treat with care: a framed print or a small murti (sacred image) from a Hindu shop or temple store. Learn to say her name: SUH-ruh-swuh-tee, with the stress on the first syllable. Choose one book, pen or instrument that matters to you; it will sit before her during this journey.
reflect: What have you learned in your life that felt like a gift rather than an achievement?
What do you already assume about Saraswati that you might need to unlearn?
further: David Kinsley, Hindu Goddesses: Visions of the Divine Feminine in the Hindu Religious Tradition (1986)
Catherine Ludvík, Sarasvatī: Riverine Goddess of Knowledge (2007)

practices.title: Set up a small, clean shrine where you learn
practices.instructions:
Choose a raised place near where you study, write or practise: a shelf or small table, never the floor, and never a bathroom. Many families keep the shrine in the north-east of the home, or keep Saraswati's image in the study. Clean the place and lay a fresh white or yellow cloth.

Set her image at the back. In front, place a small diya (oil lamp) on a heatproof plate, set well apart from any paper, an incense holder, a dish for flowers, a small plate for sweets and a cup of clean water. Beside her, place the one book, pen or instrument you chose. A small bell is customary to ring as you begin.

Keep it simple and keep it clean. Take your shoes off before you approach it, and keep your books off the floor from now on.
practices.prompt: Where did you place her shrine, and what did you set before her?

rite.title: First Lamp for Saraswati
rite.summary: A first short puja: wash, honour Ganesha, light the lamp, offer a white flower and water, set your book or instrument before her, greet her, and sit quietly.

ingredients.name: Saraswati’s image
A diya (small oil lamp) with ghee or sesame oil and a cotton wick, on a heatproof plate
One fresh white or yellow flower, such as jasmine or a marigold
A cup of clean water
A book, pen or instrument you care about
A small milk sweet or a piece of fruit
Sandalwood incense and a holder
A small bell

rite.preparation: Bathe or wash your hands, feet and face, and put on clean clothes, white or yellow if you have them. Remove your shoes. Clean the shrine and wipe your book or instrument with a clean cloth. Do not eat meat or drink alcohol beforehand. Sit on a mat or cushion before the image.

steps.title: Settle
steps.instructions: Sit quietly before her. Join your palms at your chest and take a few slow breaths.

steps.title: Ganesha first
steps.instructions: Ring the bell gently. Many Hindus honour Ganesha first at the start of any puja. Bow to him in your mind, or before his image if you have one.
steps.spoken: Ganesha, remover of obstacles, I bow to you first.

steps.title: Light the lamp
steps.instructions: Light the diya, then the incense, keeping both clear of the book.

steps.title: Offer
steps.instructions: Offer water by holding the cup up a little and setting it down. Place the flower at her feet. Then take your book, pen or instrument in both hands, touch it to your forehead, and lay it before her. Flowers are offered whole and unsmelled.
steps.spoken:
Saraswati, goddess of speech and learning,
I bow to you.
Accept this water, this flower,
and the work of my hands and mind.

steps.title: Greet her
steps.instructions: Tell her simply who you are and why you have come: to learn, and to learn how to learn.

steps.title: Sit
steps.instructions: Look at her image in the lamplight, then close your eyes for a few minutes. Let your mind grow quiet.

steps.title: Close
steps.instructions: Bow with joined palms. Let the lamp burn while you are present, then put it out gently by covering it rather than blowing it out. Leave the book before her until tomorrow.
steps.spoken: Thank you, Mother. I will come again.

rite.closing: Leave the flower until it wilts, then place it in a plant pot or garden. Pour the water onto a plant. Eat the sweet as prasad if you offered one. Tomorrow, take the book back with a bow and use it. Write a few lines in your journal.
rite.safety: Set the diya and incense on a heatproof plate away from books, paper, curtains and cloth, and never leave them unattended. Keep flame and smoke away from pets and children.

stages.title: River, Word and Teacher
stages.intro: Three lessons: Saraswati in the Vedas, as river and as speech; how her worship spread, from the Puranas to Jain and Buddhist Asia; and her festivals, Vasant Panchami and the Saraswati Puja of Navaratri. Light the lamp and offer a flower before you study each day.

lessons.title: River and Speech
lessons.summary: The great river of the Rig Veda, the goddess of sacred speech, and the river that flows unseen.

sections.heading: The best of rivers
sections.body:
In the Rig Veda, the oldest Hindu scripture, Saraswati is a mighty river, flowing from the mountains to the sea, and a goddess who nourishes, purifies and gives children and wealth. A whole hymn (Book 6, Hymn 61) praises her as a river that breaks the hills with her waves. Another verse (Book 2, Hymn 41, verse 16) calls her, in Ralph Griffith's 1889 translation, "Best Mother, best of Rivers, best of Goddesses", and asks her to give renown to people who feel of little worth.

On her banks, the hymns say, sacrifices were offered and the hymns themselves were sung. A river where sacred words were spoken became, in time, the goddess of the words.

sections.heading: Vac, the sacred word
sections.body:
In the Brahmanas, the ritual texts that follow the Vedic hymns, Saraswati is again and again identified with Vac, speech. Vac is a great goddess in her own right in the Rig Veda: in a famous hymn (Book 10, Hymn 125) she speaks in the first person, saying that she moves with all the gods and that whoever she loves she makes wise. Speech was holy because the hymns were holy; the right word, rightly spoken, held the world together.

As Saraswati and Vac merged, the river goddess became the goddess of speech, then of all learning, poetry, music and the arts. That is the Saraswati most Hindus know today.

sections.heading: The river that flows unseen
sections.body:
Later texts say the Saraswati river vanished into the desert. A common belief holds that she still flows underground and joins the Ganga and Yamuna at Prayagraj, at the Triveni Sangam, "the meeting of three", where pilgrims bathe at the Kumbh Mela. Many devotees see that hidden river as a picture of knowledge itself, flowing beneath the surface of things.

Where the Vedic river ran is debated. Many scholars and geologists identify it with the Ghaggar-Hakra, a now mostly seasonal river system in north-west India and Pakistan, once larger; others disagree, and the question has become entangled with arguments about early Indian history. It is good to know the debate exists, and not to treat any one answer as settled.

sections.heading: Brahma’s consort, Durga’s daughter
sections.body:
In the Puranas Saraswati becomes the consort of Brahma, the creator, and is sometimes said to have come forth from him: creation needs knowledge and the word. Brahma has few temples, and Saraswati, though loved everywhere, also has fewer temples than many deities; she is worshipped above all in schools, homes and at her festival.

In Bengal she is one of Durga's children, standing beside her mother with her swan in the Durga Puja images. In the later tradition of the Devi Mahatmya, the third of its three stories is assigned to Mahasaraswati, the Goddess as wisdom. These pictures sit together without strain; Hindu storytelling holds many of them at once.

knowAndDont.known: Rig Veda 6.61 and 2.41.16–18 praise the river Saraswati (Griffith, 1889); Rig Veda 10.125 is the hymn of Vac; the Brahmanas identify Saraswati with Vac; the Puranas make her Brahma’s consort; the belief in her hidden flow to the Triveni Sangam is widely held.
knowAndDont.unknown: Which river the Rig Veda meant, and when it dried, is disputed between geologists, archaeologists and historians, and the debate is politically charged. How exactly a river goddess became the goddess of speech can be traced in the texts but not dated closely.

lessons.inPractice: Read Rig Veda 6.61 and 10.125 in Griffith’s public-domain translation this week, one a day, sitting before her lamp. You are reading to learn, not reciting; Vedic recitation has its own strict rules and is learned from a teacher. Write down one line each day that stays with you. If you live near a river, go and listen to it once this week.
reflect: A river where words were spoken became the goddess of words. What place has shaped how you think or speak?
What knowledge in your life flows underground, unseen but still there?
further: Ralph T. H. Griffith, trans., The Hymns of the Rigveda (Benares, 1889–92; public domain), Book 2, Hymn 41; Book 6, Hymn 61; Book 10, Hymn 125
Catherine Ludvík, Sarasvatī: Riverine Goddess of Knowledge (2007)

lessons.title: Temples, Teachers and Far Shores
lessons.summary: Where she is worshipped, the guru and the first letter, and Saraswati among Jains and in Buddhist Asia.

sections.heading: Her temples
sections.body:
Saraswati has fewer great temples than some deities, and those she has are loved. At Basar in Telangana, on the Godavari, the Gnana Saraswati temple is famous for Akshara Abhyasam, the ceremony in which small children write their first letters. At Sringeri in Karnataka she is Sharadamba, at the monastery traditionally founded by the teacher Adi Shankara. At Koothanur in Tamil Nadu and at Panachikkadu in Kerala, families bring children to begin their learning, especially at Navaratri. The Mookambika temple at Kollur, in Karnataka, is another great place of Vidyarambham, "the beginning of learning".

In old Kashmir, Sharada Peeth, now a ruin in Pakistan-administered Kashmir, was a famous seat of the goddess and of learning; the Sharada script of Kashmir is named after her.

sections.heading: The guru and the first letter
sections.body:
In Hindu thought knowledge is passed from teacher to student, and the teacher (guru) is honoured almost as God. Saraswati and the guru are often honoured together. Guru Purnima, the full moon of Ashadha in June or July, is kept for teachers and for the sage Vyasa, said to have arranged the Vedas.

The beginning of learning is a rite of its own. At Vidyarambham or Akshara Abhyasam, a priest, teacher or elder holds a small child's finger and writes the first letters in a tray of rice; in Kerala the first letters are often also traced on the child's tongue with a gold ring. In Bengal, Hate Khori, "chalk in hand", is done at Saraswati Puja. Adults beginning a new art or course of study sometimes keep the same custom.

sections.heading: Music, poetry and the arts
sections.body:
Musicians and dancers across India begin their practice and performances by honouring Saraswati and their gurus. In Carnatic music she is the patron of the veena, and composers such as Muthuswami Dikshitar wrote songs in her praise. Poets begin long works by invoking her. A short prayer to her, beginning "Ya kundendu", praising her as white as the jasmine, the moon and snow, is sung in many North Indian schools at morning assembly.

A well-loved story says that the poet Kalidasa was a dull, unlearned man until the Goddess blessed him with speech; most versions name Kali, others Saraswati. The point is the same: the gift of the word is grace.

sections.heading: Beyond Hinduism
sections.body:
Jains honour Saraswati as Shrutadevi, the goddess of their scriptures, and some of the most beautiful images of her are Jain, such as the marble Saraswati from Pallu in Rajasthan, now in the National Museum in New Delhi. Buddhists honour her too: she appears in the Golden Light Sutra (Suvarnaprabhasa Sutra), and with it travelled across Asia. In Myanmar she is Thurathadi; in China, Biancaitian; in Japan, Benzaiten, a goddess of music, eloquence and water, with shrines on islands and by ponds.

Each of these is its own living tradition. They show how far she has travelled. They do not make her a generic "goddess of creativity" detached from Hinduism, where she remains living and loved.

knowAndDont.known: The temples at Basar, Sringeri, Koothanur, Panachikkadu and Kollur, the ruins of Sharada Peeth, Guru Purnima, Vidyarambham and Hate Khori, her place in Carnatic and Hindustani music, and Saraswati in Jain worship, the Golden Light Sutra, and as Benzaiten in Japan are documented.
knowAndDont.unknown: Foundation legends of many temples, including Sringeri’s founding by Shankara, are traditional. The authorship of popular prayers such as the "Ya kundendu" hymn is uncertain. The Kalidasa story is a legend told in several versions.

lessons.inPractice: Find out whether a temple, school or cultural centre near you keeps Saraswati Puja, or offers classes in Indian music, dance or language. If you have, or once had, a teacher who shaped you, write them a letter of thanks this week, even if you cannot send it.
reflect: Who were the teachers who gave you something you still use every day?
What new thing would you like to begin learning, as a child begins with a first letter?
further: Diana L. Eck, India: A Sacred Geography (2012)
John Stratton Hawley and Donna Marie Wulff, eds., Devī: Goddesses of India (1996)

lessons.title: Vasant Panchami and Navaratri
lessons.summary: Her spring festival in yellow, the last days of Navaratri, and books laid before her.

sections.heading: Vasant Panchami
sections.body:
Vasant Panchami, "the fifth of spring", falls on the fifth day of the bright half of the lunar month Magha, in January or February. It is Saraswati's great day across North and East India, and in Nepal. Schools and colleges hold Saraswati Puja, students set their books, pens and instruments before her image, and many do not study that day: the books are hers until they are taken back.

It is a festival of yellow, for the mustard flowers then blooming in the fields of the north. People wear yellow, cook yellow food such as saffron rice and sweet boondi, and offer yellow flowers. In the Punjab kites fill the sky. Many families choose the day to begin a child's learning, or to start any new study.

sections.heading: Saraswati Puja in Bengal
sections.body:
In West Bengal, Bangladesh, Assam and Odisha, Saraswati Puja on Vasant Panchami is the festival of students. Clay images of the goddess, white and serene on her swan, are made by potters and worshipped in homes, schools, colleges and neighbourhood pandals. Young people dress up, girls often in yellow saris, and offer flowers in a pushpanjali led by the priest. Little children are given chalk and a slate for Hate Khori, their first letters.

Many Bengali students will not eat kul, the Indian jujube fruit then in season, until it has first been offered to Saraswati. The next day the books are taken back, and the image is immersed in water, as Durga's is in autumn.

sections.heading: The last days of Navaratri
sections.body:
In South India, Saraswati is worshipped in the last days of Navaratri, the autumn "nine nights" of the Goddess. In many traditions the nine nights are divided into three, for Durga, Lakshmi and Saraswati, and Saraswati takes the last. On the ninth day, Ayudha Puja, people honour the tools of their work: books, instruments, pens, computers, vehicles and machines are cleaned, decorated and worshipped.

In Kerala, books and instruments are laid before her on the evening of the eighth day (Pooja Vaippu) and not touched until the morning of Vijayadashami, the tenth, when they are taken back (Pooja Eduppu) and children begin their letters in Vidyarambham. In Tamil Nadu and Karnataka, the golu dolls of Navaratri often include Saraswati.

sections.heading: Gentle on the water
sections.body:
As with Durga and Ganesha, clay images of Saraswati are immersed after her puja. Images made with Plaster of Paris and chemical paints pollute rivers and lakes, and many communities have returned to unbaked natural clay and natural colours, or immerse in tanks made for the purpose.

If you keep a small clay image for her festival, immerse it at home in a bucket of water, and pour the water and clay onto your garden when it has dissolved. A framed print, which is not immersed, is entirely traditional for a home shrine.

knowAndDont.known: Vasant Panchami on Magha Shukla Panchami, its yellow colours and Saraswati Puja, Bengali customs of pushpanjali, Hate Khori and waiting to eat kul, Ayudha Puja, Kerala’s Pooja Vaippu and Vidyarambham on Vijayadashami, and the immersion of clay images are widely kept and documented.
knowAndDont.unknown: How and when Vasant Panchami became her festival is not well dated; in some regions the day also honours Kama, the god of love, and the coming of spring. Customs of how many days the books rest, and on which tithi, differ by region and family.

lessons.inPractice: Mark the next Vasant Panchami and Navaratri from a panchang or a temple website. If you live near a Hindu or Bengali community, look for a Saraswati Puja you can visit: dress respectfully, remove your shoes where others do, and accept prasad with your right hand. If you can, wear something yellow that day.
reflect: Students lay their books down for a day so that the goddess can bless them. What would it be like to rest from your work and give it back for a day?
Ayudha Puja honours tools. Which tools of your life deserve thanks?
further: Rachel Fell McDermott, Revelry, Rivalry, and Longing for the Goddesses of Bengal (2011)
C. J. Fuller, The Camphor Flame: Popular Hinduism and Society in India (1992; revised 2004), on festivals

practices.title: Lamp, flower and study each day
practices.instructions: Each day, wash, light the diya and offer a flower and a cup of water. Touch your book, pen or instrument to your forehead, then study or practise with full attention for at least twenty minutes, as an offering.
practices.prompt: One line: what did you learn or practise today?

stages.title: Seven Days of Learning
stages.intro: For seven days you will offer your study, speech and art to Saraswati, rest your books before her for a day, and on the seventh take them back and begin again with a first letter. If you can, keep these days ending on Vasant Panchami or Vijayadashami; otherwise end on a Thursday or any day you begin something new. First read the lesson on honouring her at home.

lessons.title: Honouring Her at Home Today
lessons.summary: Her offerings, her days, words and mantras, customs of respect, and the sensitive points.

sections.heading: White and yellow, books and music
sections.body:
Saraswati's flowers are white and yellow: the white lotus above all, jasmine, white chrysanthemums, marigolds, and in Bengal the flame-orange palash. Her foods are white or golden and simple: kheer (rice pudding), milk sweets, curd, saffron rice, boondi, and fruit in season. All offerings are vegetarian and offered untasted. A ghee lamp and sandalwood incense are traditional.

Her truest offering is your own work. Devotees place books, pens and instruments before her, and offer study, music and honest effort. A student who works hard and a musician who practises are, in a real sense, already worshipping her.

sections.heading: Her days
sections.body:
Vasant Panchami and the last days of Navaratri are her great days. Some devotees, especially students, honour her on Thursday (Guruvar), the day of the teacher, and others on the fifth day of the bright fortnight; customs differ, so ask a family or temple near you. Guru Purnima is a good day to honour both her and your teachers.

And she is honoured at every beginning of learning: the first day of school, a first music lesson, the start of an exam, a new course of study, a book you have long meant to write.

sections.heading: Words and mantras
sections.body:
Hindus pray to Saraswati in their own words, in bhajans, in school prayers like the "Ya kundendu" hymn and the Saraswati Vandana, in stotras (hymns), and with mantras. Short name-mantras of Saraswati are widely heard. Some mantras, though, are traditionally given by a guru, with instruction in how and when to say them, and some, such as those for the beginning of learning, are given in a rite by a priest or teacher. Those are not given here.

You can pray freely in your own language and say her names: Saraswati, Sharada, Vani, Bharati, Vagdevi. If you want to recite in Sanskrit, ask a priest, teacher or Hindu friend; pronunciation matters, and to a goddess of speech perhaps most of all.

sections.heading: Customs of respect, and sensitive points
sections.body:
Remove your shoes before her shrine. Offer with the right hand or both hands, food untasted and flowers unsmelled. Keep meat, eggs and alcohol away from the shrine. Keep her image raised, clean and out of bathrooms. Keep books, paper and instruments off the floor and away from your feet; if you touch one with your foot, touch it with your hand and then to your forehead.

The sensitive point with Saraswati is easy to miss: she is often treated as a "goddess of creativity" in wellness and art circles, cut off from her own religion. Honour her as Hindus do, and remember that most Hindus first meet her as children at school, with real love. Above all, go to a Saraswati Puja, and find a good teacher.

knowAndDont.known: White and yellow flowers, milk sweets, books and instruments as her offerings, Vasant Panchami and Navaratri as her festivals, Guru Purnima for teachers, the school prayers to her, and the customs of respect toward books are widespread in living practice.
knowAndDont.unknown: There is no single correct home puja, and no single weekly day for her everywhere; customs differ by family, region and tradition. Views on who may chant which mantras vary within Hinduism.

lessons.inPractice: Gather white or yellow flowers, a small sweet, and the books, pens or instrument you use most. Choose which day will be your seventh, and plan something new to begin on it: a book, a course, a song, a language.
reflect: If your daily work were an offering, what would you do differently?
Where have you seen her image used carelessly, and how did it feel to notice it?
further: Diana L. Eck, Darśan: Seeing the Divine Image in India (1981)
C. J. Fuller, The Camphor Flame (1992; revised 2004)

practices.title: Seven days of learning
practices.instructions:
Each day: wash, ring the bell, light the diya (well clear of any paper) and incense, and offer water, a white or yellow flower and a little sweet or fruit. Touch your book or instrument to your forehead. Then give the day's practice your full attention, and write a few lines.

Day 1, speech: speak only what is true and kind today, and notice how often that is hard. Day 2, reading: read slowly from a good book or a scripture in translation, such as a chapter of the Bhagavad Gita or a hymn of the Rig Veda. Day 3, writing: write a page by hand, carefully. Day 4, music: sing, play, or listen to a raga or bhajan with full attention. Day 5, craft: make something with your hands, as well as you can. Day 6, rest: in the evening lay your books, pens and instrument before her, and do not study; thank your teachers instead, in words or a letter.

Day 7, beginning: in the morning, bow and take your books back. Spread a little uncooked rice on a clean plate and, with your finger, write in it the first letter of something you are beginning, or simply "Om" or her name. Then begin that new thing. Afterwards, give the rice to birds or add it to your cooking.
practices.prompt: What did today’s practice teach you, and what did it ask of you?

stages.title: After the First Letter
stages.intro: Take a few days with only the daily lamp, flower and study. Reread your journal. A vow of devotion is one good outcome; so is pausing, learning more at a temple or from a teacher first, or finding that your path lies elsewhere. An honest answer is itself a kind of knowledge.

practices.title: Read your journal back
practices.instructions: Read your journal from the first lamp. Note what drew you, what surprised you, and what you learned from people rather than from screens. Then answer the questions below.
practices.prompt: What has this month taught you about Saraswati, and about how you learn?

questions: Are you drawn to Saraswati herself, as Hindus worship her, or to the idea of a goddess who helps you pass exams or be creative? Be honest; only the first is what this vow is for.
Can you keep a small, clean daily practice (a lamp, a flower, study offered to her) and the customs of respect toward books and teachers through an ordinary year?
Have you visited a temple or a Saraswati Puja, or spoken with Hindu devotees? If not, would it be better to do that before any vow?
Would learning from a Hindu teacher or community, in time, serve your devotion better than a self-made vow? A vow now does not stop you doing that later.
If you decide to wait, or stop, can you offer her a last flower with thanks, and keep honouring your books and teachers? That is a good ending too.

stages.title: A Vow of Devotion
stages.intro: If you choose to go on, this is a personal vow of devotion to Saraswati, made in a simple puja. It is not dīkṣā, not an initiation into any Hindu tradition or lineage, and does not replace one; it does not make you a member of a sampradaya or give you anything a guru gives. It is your own promise of bhakti. Vasant Panchami, Vijayadashami, Guru Purnima or a Thursday are fitting days.

rite.title: Vow of Devotion to Saraswati
rite.summary: A full home puja with white and yellow flowers, your books and instrument laid before her, honouring Ganesha first, your own vow (sankalpa) of devotion and study, arati and the sharing of prasad.

ingredients.name: Saraswati’s image, cleaned and garlanded if you can
A fresh white or yellow cloth for the shrine
A diya with ghee and a cotton wick, on a heatproof plate
A plate for the arati lamp
White and yellow flowers, such as jasmine and marigolds, or a small garland
Sandalwood paste or a little sandalwood oil
Incense and a holder
Kheer, a milk sweet or saffron rice, and fruit
A cup of clean water
Your books, pens or instrument
A little uncooked rice on a clean plate
A small bell
Your vow, written by hand on clean paper

rite.preparation:
During the day, write your vow by hand, carefully. Keep it honest and keepable: what you will do (a daily lamp and an hour of study or practice offered to her, respect for books and teachers, her festivals, a temple visit), what you will learn or teach, for how long (a year is common), and what you ask of her. Many people include a promise of service, such as teaching someone what they know, or giving books to those who have none.

Bathe, dress in clean clothes (white or yellow if you like), and remove your shoes. Clean the shrine and lay the fresh cloth. Wipe your books and instrument with a clean cloth. Prepare the food without tasting it.

steps.title: Begin with Ganesha
steps.instructions: Sit before the shrine. Join your palms and breathe. Ring the bell. Honour Ganesha first with a flower and a bow.
steps.spoken: Ganesha, remover of obstacles, I bow to you first.

steps.title: Light and fragrance
steps.instructions: Light the diya and incense, clear of books and paper. Touch a little sandalwood paste to the base of her image or its frame.

steps.title: Flowers and names
steps.instructions: Offer the flowers one at a time, saying one of her names with each.
steps.spoken: Saraswati. Sharada. Vani. Bharati. Vagdevi. Vidyadayini. Veenapani…

steps.title: Lay down your work
steps.instructions: Take your books, pens or instrument one by one, touch each to your forehead, and lay them before her.
steps.spoken:
Mother, all I know I received.
I lay my work before you.
Make my mind clear and my speech true.

steps.title: Food and water
steps.instructions: Set the sweet and fruit before her, with the cup of water. Sprinkle a few drops of water around the food.
steps.spoken: This food is yours, Mother. Accept it, and let it come back to us as your grace.

steps.title: The vow
steps.instructions: Take a little water in your right palm. Read your vow aloud, slowly and clearly. Let the water fall onto the plate beneath her, as a sign that the intention is made. Place the paper at her feet.

steps.title: A first letter
steps.instructions: With your finger, write in the rice the first letter of what you will learn this year, or her name.

steps.title: Arati
steps.instructions: Light the arati lamp from the diya. Wave it slowly in clockwise circles before her, from her feet to her face, while you sing or hum. Then pass your hands over the flame and touch them to your eyes and the top of your head.

steps.title: Sit with her
steps.instructions: Sit in silence before her for a while. Let your mind grow still and clear.

steps.title: Close and share prasad
steps.instructions: Bow with joined palms. Take a little of the sweet as prasad and share the rest today. Let the lamp burn while you are present, then cover it gently. Leave the books before her until tomorrow morning.
steps.spoken: Thank you, Mother. I will keep learning, and I will keep my word.

rite.closing: Keep your vow folded near her shrine and read it each Vasant Panchami. The next morning, take your books back with a bow and study. Give the rice to birds or cook with it. Share the prasad. Return flowers to the earth. Write the date in your journal. If you can, thank a teacher in the coming week, in person.
rite.safety: Keep the diya, arati lamp and incense on heatproof plates, away from books, paper, cloth, garlands, hair and loose sleeves, and never leave them unattended. If you use camphor for arati, burn only a small piece on a metal plate, keep it from children and pets, and never eat it.

stages.title: A Life of Learning
stages.intro: After the vow, devotion is daily and yearly: a lamp and study offered to her, respect for books and teachers, Vasant Panchami and Navaratri, temple visits, and a yearly renewal of your vow.

practices.title: Daily lamp and study
practices.instructions: Each day, wash, light the lamp, offer a flower and water, bow, and study or practise with full attention as an offering.

practices.title: A day for teachers each month
practices.instructions: Once a month, on a Thursday or the Purnima (check a panchang), offer a fuller puja with white or yellow flowers and a sweet, and do one thing for learning: thank a teacher, teach someone what you know, or give a book away.
practices.prompt: What did you learn, and what did you pass on, this month?

practices.title: Vasant Panchami and Navaratri
practices.instructions: Each year, keep Vasant Panchami in January or February: wear yellow, lay your books before her for the day, and visit a Saraswati Puja if you can. In the autumn, at the end of Navaratri, lay your books and tools before her again, and on Vijayadashami take them back and begin something new.
practices.prompt: What did you begin this festival, and who did you learn from?

practices.title: Yearly renewal
practices.instructions: On the anniversary of your vow, or at Vasant Panchami, reread it, write it anew by hand, and repeat the vow puja. Change it honestly. If you are ending it, offer a last flower and sweet with thanks, take down the shrine with care, and give the image to a temple or immerse a clay image respectfully.
practices.prompt: What has a year of learning with Saraswati changed in you?
